new mexico.enforce_note: Non-competes are banned only for covered health care practitioners, while other employees' non-competes are allowed if reasonable under case law.
new mexico.state_note: A covered health care practitioner's non-compete is unenforceable once the job ends, and any clause forcing the dispute into another state's law or courts is void, though limited repayment and liquidated-damages terms can still apply.
new mexico.threshold_note: New Mexico sets no earnings threshold; the ban turns on the worker's profession, not pay.

new york.enforce_note: New York has no general non-compete statute, so courts enforce non-competes only when they pass the strict reasonableness test from BDO Seidman v. Hirshberg.
new york.state_note: A broad ban passed the Senate in 2023 but was vetoed by the governor, and the 2026 Senate-passed bill stalled in the Assembly, so the court test still governs and a separate narrow ban covers only broadcast-industry employees.
new york.threshold_note: New York sets no earnings threshold; the $500,000 threshold in pending bills is not law.

north carolina.enforce_note: North Carolina enforces a non-compete only if it is in writing, supported by consideration, reasonable in time and territory, and protects a legitimate business interest.
north carolina.state_note: The agreement must be in writing and signed to be enforceable at all, and a court may only strike a separable overbroad part rather than rewrite the clause.
north carolina.threshold_note: North Carolina sets no earnings threshold; enforceability turns on the five-part common-law reasonableness test.

north dakota.enforce_note: Every contract restraining someone from exercising a lawful profession, trade, or business is void, so employee non-competes are unenforceable for all workers.
north dakota.state_note: Employers cannot get around the ban by writing another state's law or forum into the contract, because North Dakota courts refuse to enforce choice-of-law clauses used to evade the ban.
north dakota.statute_name: Contracts in Restraint of Trade Void
north dakota.threshold_note: There is no earnings threshold because the ban covers every employee regardless of pay, with narrow exceptions only for the sale of a business's goodwill or the dissolution of a partnership, LLC, or corporation.

ohio.enforce_note: Ohio has no non-compete statute, so courts enforce non-competes only as far as they are reasonable under the Raimonde v. Van Vlerah test.
ohio.state_note: Unlike many states, an Ohio judge may rewrite an overbroad non-compete to make it reasonable and then enforce the revised version instead of throwing the whole clause out.
ohio.threshold_note: Ohio sets no earnings threshold; enforceability turns on whether the restraint is no greater than needed to protect the employer, imposes no undue hardship, and does not harm the public.

oklahoma.enforce_note: A former employee must be allowed to engage in the same or a similar business, so true non-competes are void and unenforceable for all employees.
oklahoma.state_note: The only restriction an employer can still enforce against a former employee is a ban on directly soliciting the employer's established customers.
oklahoma.threshold_note: There is no earnings threshold because the ban covers every employee regardless of pay, with narrow exceptions only for the sale of a business's goodwill or a partnership dissolution.

oregon.enforce_note: A non-compete is void unless the employee is exempt, the employer has a protectable interest, the worker got two weeks' written notice, and the worker's pay at termination exceeds the annual threshold.
oregon.state_note: The non-compete can last no more than 12 months, and an employer can still enforce one against a lower-paid worker only by paying garden leave of at least 50 percent of the worker's pay while the restriction runs.
oregon.threshold_note: For 2026 the threshold is $119,541 in annual gross salary and commissions at termination, and it is re-indexed every year for inflation using the CPI for All Urban Consumers, West Region.

pennsylvania.enforce_note: Pennsylvania has no general non-compete statute, so most non-competes are judged under a court reasonableness test, but health care practitioners have special statutory limits since January 1, 2025.
pennsylvania.state_note: For covered health care practitioners, a non-compete signed on or after January 1, 2025 is void if it lasts more than one year or if the employer dismissed the practitioner, and the employer must notify the practitioner's patients within 90 days of departure.
pennsylvania.statute_name: Fair Contracting for Health Care Practitioners Act
pennsylvania.threshold_note: Pennsylvania sets no earnings threshold; the health care limits turn on the worker's profession and how the job ended, not pay.

rhode island.enforce_note: Non-competes are unenforceable against nonexempt workers, workers age 18 or younger, students and interns, and low-wage employees, while higher-paid workers can still be bound if the clause is reasonable.
rhode island.state_note: A 2025 bill that would have voided non-competes for everyone earning under $125,000 passed the Senate but died without a House vote, so the 250-percent-of-poverty-level line still governs.
rhode island.threshold_note: For 2026 a low-wage employee is one earning no more than 250 percent of the federal poverty level for an individual, about $39,900, and the figure moves each year when the federal poverty guidelines change.

south carolina.enforce_note: South Carolina has no non-compete statute, so courts enforce non-competes only when they protect a legitimate business interest, are reasonable in time and territory, are not unduly harsh, and rest on valuable consideration.
south carolina.state_note: South Carolina courts will not trim or rewrite an overbroad clause, so a single unreasonable term voids the entire non-compete, and a worker asked to sign mid-employment must get new consideration beyond just keeping the job.
south carolina.threshold_note: South Carolina sets no earnings threshold; enforceability turns on the common-law test, not pay.
